doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Narrating solos and what he thinks about while playing
summary: Levy discusses a narrated-solo video, awareness of the rhythm section, polyrhythms in Sweet Pomegranates, interval shapes and engaging the audience.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about a video that I could only find once. It was very interesting because you were playing – it might even have been not in an established band – but you had an extended solo and after the fact you were talking about what you were doing. And you were saying, “Okay listen to this now I’m doing this scale in arpeggios,” or “I’m playing a little blues lick here” and at one point you quoted another song and it was interesting because it was like your own narration of what you were doing. Do you remember this video?
Like a lot of musicians, “No I don’t remember doing that” but –
Oh yeah that wedding you played with me forty years ago, I’m sure I was there but I don’t remember. No I have so many videos out and I film so many things at my house
that are actually on my YouTube channel and I’m actually very proud of it. But that particular one – if you showed it to me I’m sure that I would remember it.

Well what made me think and wonder, when you were doing these things you were describing after the fact, how conscious of them were you doing in real time? In other words what do you think about, are you intentionally “I’m going to play this now” you know in a split second and you do?
Oh I think I know what you’re talking about, yes. This is something – I put up a video recently. My wife said, “Hey why don’t you narrate your solo?”

Yeah we put up captions. And yeah, well all of that stuff is going on – the mind operates on many, and the spirit operates on many different levels when you’re playing. And a lot of it is interacting with the people you’re playing with. And I’m always – I think the fact that I’m a pianist, when I’m playing harmonica I really interact with the rhythm section in a way that’s very, very direct and personal because I was a rhythm section player before I was a wind instrument player. So I’m very, very aware of rhythmic interplay. And also I listen to like every note that everyone else is playing. Always. I’m aware of all the like bass players’ bass lines. I know what they’re doing. And if I close my eyes I can see what the piano player is doing and see his hands, and that kind of stuff. So that’s one level of what’s going on. And the other level is how I’m interacting with that and the structure of the tune, if it’s a tune with changes. You know? And so oh yeah, I’m very conscious of these kind of mathematical things as I’m doing them. But sometimes there are things I’ve worked on, like I remember I was playing triplets in fours – it’s just something that’s like feeling but I stepped back from it at a certain point and said, “Oh yeah I’m playing instead of [scats] I’m going [scats]” you know that kind of thing. And I work on these things. I mean I just work on so much stuff and rhythmic ratios. If I’m playing a tune that’s like an ostinato, this tune that I wrote that we do in the Flecktones called “Sweet Pomegranates.” It’s an ostinato in six and it’s in G sharp minor, an ostinato pattern in the left hand that I play the whole time with – I can’t demonstrate it in the air but so I figured out how to play in five against that six, and in seven against that six, and nine against it and eleven against it. And I started gradually working it into my solos live at a certain point, inspired by Indian music really, where they do stuff like that all the time. And so yeah there’s a certain amount of calculation in my playing, and the interaction, and also sometimes just going for it, just the shapes of intervals. Just almost like a line drawing you know. Because intervals have shapes. And if people just learn how to play jazz by learning your modes and your scales, I mean that’s cool. That’s sort of a reference framework. But to make a real artistic statement there’s way more to it than just what are the correct notes and the relationship of those notes to the harmonic framework. There’s

the shape of what you’re doing. So I’m very conscious of that, and building tension in a solo. And if I’m playing live trying to engage the audience too. Reach out to them. Because I feel lucky to be able to have an audience you know. And so I want to give them back like as much as I possibly can. I want to take them on a journey you know.
